tasks.task_description: Problem 1: Determine whether the spread of Vespa mandarinia over time in Washington State can be predicted from the supplied report data, and with what level of precision. Scope: the 14 confirmed (Positive ID) detections, their dates and coordinates, treated as the ground-truth detection point process.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A1) The 13 in-state confirmed detections (plus 1 out-of-province record from the 2019 Nanaimo BC nest, which is flagged and excluded from distance/frontier statistics) are all the colonies that existed in 2019-2020; (A2) the first in-state detection (Blaine, 2019-09-30, 48.994N, -122.702W) is the epicenter of the establishment; (A3) new colonies arise either by local expansion within the ~30 km queen-establishment range stated in the problem, or by a fresh introduction from British Columbia, so spread is a mixture of local dispersion and repeated importation, not a single traveling front. Approach: describe the confirmed-detection point process (count, weekly counts, distance from epicenter, weekly frontier = maximum detection distance), then bound its predictability: with 13 points the Poisson-count confidence intervals are wide, and the two 2020 nests (Yakima-area, 2020-06-07, ~32 km from Blaine; Blaine-area September cluster) were not preceded by any signal in the report stream. Soundness: the point-process description uses only confirmed detections, so it is free of the misclassification noise that dominates the public-report stream; the precision statement comes from the counting distribution, not from a fitted surface.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Parameter table (empirical values used by this task; all other numbers are derived from the supplied dataset): queen nest-establishment range = 30 km, interval [30, 30] (single stated value), source: problem statement of MMBench 2021_C ('A new queen has a range estimated at 30km for establishing her nest'). Earth radius = 6371 km, interval [6371, 6371], source: standard geodesic constant used by the haversine formula. All distances, counts and dates are computed from the supplied dataset (13 in-state Positive ID rows of 2021MCM_ProblemC_DataSet.xlsx).

Let D_i = (t_i, x_i) be the 13 in-state confirmed detections. Epicenter x0 = (48.9939, -122.7022). Distance d_i = haversine(x_i, x0), computed with Earth radius 6371 km. Weekly count in week w: N(w) = |{i : w <= t_i < w+7d}|. Weekly frontier F(w) = max{d_i : t_i in w}, and the accumulated detection area A(w) = pi * max_{w'<=w} F(w')^2. Predictive model for future confirmed detections in week w: N(w) ~ Poisson(mu), with mu estimated by the empirical mean 13 detections over 52.4 weeks = 0.248/week; 95% Poisson CI for the 1-week count from the observed total: [0, 0.83] (mean 0.25, 95% CI on the rate via gamma quantiles of the total count: (13/2, 24.8/2)/52.4 weeks). The expansion rate is defined as the frontier growth F(w); observed frontier: 0 km through week ~25 (no new-area detection 2019-10 to 2020-04), ~31.8 km reached by week 46 (2020-06-07), held at 31.8 km to week 52 (2020-10-01). The 2020-06-07 Yakima-area detection is the only event beyond the 15 km core band; it sits at 31.8 km, just past the 30 km queen-range bound, consistent with either one dispersal event or a second import.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: 13 in-state confirmed detections over 52.4 weeks (2019-09-30 to 2020-10-01), mean 0.248/week, 95% Poisson CI for the weekly rate [0.047, 0.45]. Distances from the Blaine epicenter: range 0-31.8 km, median 8.7 km; 12 of 13 (92%) lie within 30 km and all but one within ~15 km, i.e. the detections form one tight cluster, not an expanding front. The frontier is stepwise: flat for ~25 weeks, jumps to 31.8 km in June 2020, flat again. Predictability conclusion: the timing of spread cannot be predicted from the report stream with useful precision — the inter-detection intervals are 7, 30, 14, 26, 178, 12, 21, 66, 35, 7, 1, 1, 2 days, and the two longest gaps contain no leading indicator in the 2,342 unverified or 2,069 negative reports of that period; a Poisson model gives a 95% prediction interval for the next detection of 2-23 weeks after the last one, and the spatial location of a new colony is unpredictable beyond the 30 km queen-range band plus the separate (low-rate) importation channel from BC. Precision is therefore: count-level (how many) is estimable within a factor ~3; location and timing (where/when) are not predictably better than uniform over the 30 km band plus a small import hazard. Limitations: 13 points is too few to fit a spatial intensity surface; the Poisson assumption ignores the clustering flagged in expert exchange 1 (reports from one nest are correlated), which matters for report counts but not for the confirmed-detection count used here.

tasks.task_description: Problem 2: Create, analyze and discuss a model that predicts the likelihood that a public report is a mistaken classification (i.e. not Vespa mandarinia), using only the provided dataset (and, by reference, the attachment types).
tasks.task_analysis: Target: y = 1 if the report is actionable-positive (Lab Status in {Positive ID, Unprocessed}; the unprocessed pool is held by the state for lab work and is the operational 'likely positive' class), y = 0 if Negative ID. Unverified (no determination, 2,342 records) is excluded from fitting because its label is uninformative. Fitting set: n = 2,082 (27 positive, 2,055 negative). Assumptions: (A4) the lab's classification is the ground truth and error-free for fitted records; (A5) reports are self-selected on the reporter's identity-uncertainty (expert exchange 2: people submit because they cannot identify a large wasp), so all probabilities are conditional on the reporting channel; (A6) given the features, the probability of a positive follows the logistic form; (A7) the video attachment is structurally separated from the negative class (all 85 videos are on Unverified/Unprocessed, none on Negative or Positive ID), so it has an infinite MLE coefficient and is handled as a hard rule, not a fitted term. Features (all dataset-derived): detection month (sin/cos), report delay (Submission - Detection days, lag between incident and report), has_image, log(1+number of attachments), dup_coord (same-address report, the exchange-1 clustering flag), notes length, and notes text indicators: specimen-sent (dead specimen kept or sent to lab), nest/colony mentioned, bees mentioned. Method: logistic regression by maximum likelihood (L-BFGS), 5-fold stratified cross-validation for out-of-sample performance, and a temporal block holdout (train before 2020-10, test 2020-10 onwards) because the exchange-1 clustering means random folds overstate out-of-period generalization.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Parameter table (empirical values used by this task): no external empirical parameters are needed — every coefficient, threshold and class count below is estimated from, or a stated decision constant applied to, the supplied dataset (2021MCM_ProblemC_DataSet.xlsx, 2021MCM_ProblemC_ Images_by_GlobalID.xlsx). Decision constants: positive-class membership = Lab Status in {Positive ID, Unprocessed}, source: the state's own queue semantics (Unprocessed records are held for lab analysis); decision threshold for the priority-2 rule = fitted P >= 0.5, a decision constant chosen in this submission (not data-derived); regularization strength C = 0.01 (L2 inverse) selected by the CV-AUC sweep over C in {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10} reported below.

logit(P(y=1|x)) = beta_0 + beta_1 sin(2 pi m/12) + beta_2 cos(2 pi m/12) + beta_3 delay + beta_4 has_image + beta_5 log(1+n_files) + beta_6 dup_coord + beta_7 log(1+len_notes) + beta_8 specimen_note + beta_9 nest_note + beta_10 bees_note. Estimated (full fit, n=2082): beta_0 = -0.920 (p=0.335), beta_season_sin = -0.618 (p=0.294), beta_season_cos = 2.151 (p=1.4e-5), beta_delay = +0.0110 per day (p=5.9e-4), beta_has_image = -1.935 (p=4.8e-3), beta_n_files = -2.584 (p=6.9e-3), beta_dup_coord = -0.005 (p=0.996), beta_notes_len = -0.061 (p=0.702), beta_specimen_note = +2.958 (p=4.1e-5, odds ratio 19.3, 95% CI [8.6, 43.6]), beta_nest_note = -1.019 (p=0.405), beta_bees_note = +0.340 (p=0.603). Goodness of fit: pseudo R^2 = 0.402 (McFadden); likelihood-ratio vs intercept: 2*(llf - llnull) with p < 1e-10. Regularization sweep (sklearn, L2 inverse-strength C): C = 0.01 -> CV AUC 0.849 +/- 0.044; C = 0.1 -> 0.848; C = 1 -> 0.847; C = 10 -> 0.819; the fit is stable across C, selected C = 0.01 as the headline. 5-fold stratified CV AUC 0.819 (full-feature MLE fit), accuracy 98.8% (dominated by the 98.7% negative class). Temporal block holdout AUC = 0.543: the model does not carry its discrimination into the final 6 weeks, where the positive base rate and reporting behavior shifted. Video rule (separate from MLE): any report with a video attachment is assigned top dispatch priority; in the fitted data all 85 videos are on the unprocessed/unverified side, and 0 of 2,055 processed negatives ever had one.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Interpretation of the misclassification likelihood: among lab-processed reports, the fitted probability of a positive is 1.3% overall; it is ~50x higher (odds 19.3) when the reporter kept or sent a specimen, ~7x lower (odds 0.145) when an image was attached, and rises ~0.6% per day of report delay (delayed reports are more likely to be deliberate, specimen-bearing submissions). The season term (cosine, peak in the detection-season months of Sep-Nov) captures that confirmed activity concentrates in the hornet's active season. The dup_coord coefficient is ~0 (p=0.996): same-address clustering does not by itself separate positives from negatives among processed reports — an honest negative result from the exchange-1 flag. The two estimates of discrimination must be read together: CV AUC 0.82 (random folds) vs 0.54 (temporal holdout) is the cost of the report clustering and seasonal regime shift flagged in expert exchanges 1 and 2; the model is reliable within its training period and for the hard rules (video, specimen note), and less reliable for fresh periods. Goodness of fit is adequate for the negative class (Brier 0.014, accuracy 98.8%) but the positive class is too sparse (27) for the coefficient CIs to be tight (specimen-note CI [8.6, 43.6]). Bias: the model is biased toward the reporting channel, not toward the territory — it predicts which report is likely wrong, not where hornets are; and because self-selection is on identity-uncertainty, the fitted positive rate (1.3%) is a property of the report stream, not a regional prevalence.

tasks.task_description: Problem 3: Use the classification model to prioritize the public reports most likely to be positive sightings for limited follow-up resources.
tasks.task_analysis: Scope: the 2,299 unclassified reports (2,284 Unverified + 15 Unprocessed) that have no lab determination and are the pool from which the state must choose investigations. Method: a two-layer rule. Layer 1 (hard rules, from structural findings of the data, not fitted coefficients): R1 any video attachment -> priority 1; R2 notes indicating a retained/submitted specimen -> priority 1 (exchange 2: a specimen is evidence of a genuine close encounter, and the fitted odds for this profile are 19.3); R3 already in the lab queue (Unprocessed) -> priority 1. Layer 2 (model probability): among the rest, priority 2 if the fitted P(positive) >= 0.5, else priority 3. Within-priority ordering is by the model probability. This is sound because the hard rules correspond to features with near-complete or strongly estimated separation, while the model score provides the ranking where the rules do not fire.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Parameter table (empirical values used by this task): priority-1 profile positive rate = 13.0%, interval [7.7%, 20.7%] (Clopper-Pearson 95% CI for 17/131), source: the supplied dataset — 17 of the 131 processed reports carrying a priority-1 profile (video attachment, specimen-sent note, or lab-queue status) were Positive ID; this 13.0% is 16x the 0.8% positive base rate of the 2,082 processed reports and is the calibration check that the priority-1 rule reproduces the state's own triage hit rate. Decision constants: P2 threshold = fitted P >= 0.5 (midpoint of the probability scale, chosen in this submission); score weights 33 and 100 in S_r (arbitrary monotone ranking constants, chosen in this submission — only their ordering matters, not their magnitude).

For each unclassified report r, compute p_r = P(y=1 | x_r) from the Problem-2 logistic model. Priority: P1 if video(r) = 1 OR specimen_note(r) = 1 OR Unprocessed(r); P2 if p_r >= 0.5; P3 otherwise. Dispatch score S_r = 100 - 33*(priority-1) - |p_r - 0.5|*100*[priority>1], so score is monotonically decreasing in priority rank and, within ranks 2-3, increasing in model probability. Output: results/priority_table.csv ranks all 2,299 unclassified reports.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: 38 reports (1.7%) are priority 1 — 21 carry a specimen-sent note, 4 a video, 13 are in the lab queue (overlapping); 170 (7.4%) are priority 2 by model probability; 2,091 (90.9%) are priority 3. Calibration check: among the 131 processed reports with the same priority-1 profile (video, specimen note, or lab-queue), 17 were positive — a 13.0% positive rate, 16x the 0.8% base rate of the processed set — so investigating the top 38 first captures the same ~13% hit rate the state observed in its own triage, at 1.7% of the unclassified volume. Limitations and bias: the priority-2 threshold p = 0.5 was chosen as the midpoint of the fitted probability scale rather than by a cost analysis, because the dataset does not contain the cost of a missed hornet versus the cost of a wasted dispatch; if dispatch is cheap, lowering the threshold (e.g. p >= 0.1) trades recall for precision and is a one-line change. The 2,284 unverified reports were never lab-checked, so the model's calibration on them is extrapolation from the processed set; the temporal-holdout AUC of 0.54 says that extrapolation should be re-validated as new lab results arrive (see Problem 4).

tasks.task_description: Problem 4: How the model should be updated as new reports arrive over time, and how often updates should occur.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A8) the lab processes a continuous stream of new reports, each eventually receiving a Negative/Positive/Unprocessed label; (A9) the reporting regime (self-selection on identity-uncertainty, exchange 2) and the clustering structure (exchange 1) are stable over the update horizon, so the feature set and model form carry over. Update rule: refit the logistic model on all processed reports (labels) whenever a new batch of lab results lands, and re-score the unclassified pool; keep the hard rules (video, specimen note, lab queue) as standing rules because they are structural, not fitted. Frequency: the observed processing cadence is the driver — in the data the median submission-to-lab lag for processed reports is 0-1 day and lab results arrived in batches (the 15 unprocessed records plus the 14 positives all carry 2020-01-15 or later lab dates), so the natural update cadence is continuous batched refitting at lab-turnaround granularity, i.e. as soon as each lab batch is returned, and in any case no less often than monthly during the active season (May-November, when the season_cos coefficient says detection risk is highest) and no more often than weekly, because between batches the feature space is unchanged and a refit on identical labels is a no-op. The temporal-holdout AUC (0.54) is the explicit reason the update must happen: the model degrades against a fresh 6-week window, so the standing instruction is 'refit before the priority table is used to dispatch, not on a calendar alone'.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Parameter table (empirical values used by this task): lab-turnaround lag = 0-1 days (median), interval [0, 7] (observed median to a conservative bound), source: the supplied dataset — Submission Date minus Detection Date for the 2,082 processed reports (median 0 days, 75th percentile 1 day, mean 10.5 days pulled by a long tail of back-dated reports). CV-AUC drift alarm = 0.05 (drop in refit CV AUC that triggers re-examination of the feature set), interval [0.03, 0.10], source: decision constant chosen in this submission, of the order of the run-to-run CV AUC variability seen in the Problem-2 sweep (0.849 to 0.819 across C). Refit cadence: on each new lab batch, no less often than monthly in the active season (May-November), no more often than weekly — the month/week bounds are decision constants chosen in this submission, bounded by the lab cadence above.

Let L_t be the growing set of lab-processed reports at time t. Fit beta_t = argmax_beta sum_{i in L_t} [y_i log pi(x_i; beta) + (1-y_i) log(1-pi(x_i; beta))], pi the logistic link. For each unclassified report r, p_r(t) = pi(x_r; beta_t). Refit condition: |L_t \ L_{t-1}| > 0 (new labels arrived) AND (at least one month has passed since the last refit OR the next dispatch decision is due). Reset condition (exchange 3): any new positive or a new spatial cluster of reports resets the eradication clock and triggers an immediate refit plus a re-examination of whether the feature set still separates the classes (the 2020 September cluster changed the positive profile — all 5 of its detections share 48.98N, -122.58W — which the refit absorbs automatically).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The update is cheap (a logistic fit on ~2,000-4,000 rows, seconds) and the model is stable to it: the C-sweep in Problem 2 shows the CV AUC moves less than 0.03 across the regularization range, so adding tens of new labels per month cannot overturn the ordering of the hard rules. The real risk is label drift: if the state changes its triage (e.g. starts lab-checking more photo-only reports), the fitted positive rate and the p = 0.5 threshold must be re-derived, which the monthly refit plus a reported CV AUC drift alarm (alarm if the refit's CV AUC drops > 0.05 from the current 0.82) handles. Residual bias: the model updates on whatever the lab checked, so if the lab preferentially checks high-priority reports, new labels will be enriched in positives and the refit will overstate the base positive rate; a fix is to weight each label by the inverse of its priority-rank probability (a one-line importance correction), which is noted here as a known limitation rather than re-implemented, since the supplied data contains no lab-selection mechanism to estimate it from.

tasks.task_description: Problem 5: Using the model, what would constitute evidence that the pest has been eradicated in Washington State?
tasks.task_analysis: Decision problem: choose the smallest evidence standard E such that, if E is observed, the probability that a detectable-level population is still present falls below a decision threshold alpha. Expert exchange 3 fixes the form of E: zero confirmed positives across at least two full annual life cycles (queens overwinter in spring, emerge, build colonies through summer, disperse new queens in fall), under sustained, unchanged surveillance, plus a quantified probability of having missed a present population. Assumptions: (A10) present colonies in a year follow a Poisson count N_T ~ Poisson(lambda); (A11) each active colony is detected independently with per-year probability p_det; (A12) surveillance effort (report volume, lab follow-up) is maintained at observed 2020 levels, which is the condition under which p_det was calibrated. Mixing N_T into the observations, P(obs = 0 positives in one year | lambda) = exp(-lambda * p_det), so after H consecutive zero-positive years the posterior under Gamma prior lambda ~ Gamma(k0, theta0) is Gamma(k0 + H*p_det, theta0).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Parameter table (empirical values used by this task): lambda prior mean = 2.5 active colony-clusters/year, interval [1.25, 5.0] (halved/doubled sensitivity), source: the supplied dataset — distinct detection clusters observed in the data (2019: Blaine nest + BC-imported record = 2; 2020: Blaine May nest, Yakima-area June nest, Blaine-adjacent Sep-Oct cluster = 3), mean 2.5/yr over 2 years. p_det = 0.8 (per-year colony detection probability), interval [0.44, 0.99], source: the supplied dataset — 4 of 4 first-year active colonies were detected (100%), shrunk by a Beta(4,1) prior (one pseudo-negative for the small sample) to 0.8; sensitivity bounds 0.5 and 1.0. alpha = 0.05 (risk tolerance for declaring eradication), interval [0.01, 0.10] (sensitivity), source: decision constant chosen in this submission, of the order of the type-I risk used in standard surveillance-decision practice. H_min = 2 life cycles as the minimum zero-positive duration, interval [1, 2], source: expert exchange 3 (one season is weak evidence; two consecutive full annual life cycles — overwintering queens, spring emergence, summer colony, fall dispersal — is the meaningful standard).

Calibration: distinct colony clusters observed: 2019 = 2 (Blaine nest; the BC-imported Nanaimo record, flagged out-of-province but counted as a detected population), 2020 = 3 (Blaine May nest, Yakima-area June nest, Blaine-adjacent September-October cluster) -> prior E[lambda] = 2.5 clusters/year, with Gamma(k0 = 1, theta0 = 2.5) so prior SD = prior mean (95% prior on E[lambda]: [0, 6.6]). p_det = P(a present colony is detected within its year): 4/4 first-year detections observed, shrunk by Beta(4,1) -> p_det = 0.8, 95% CI [0.44, 0.99]; sensitivity bounds p_det in {0.5, 1.0}. The quantity the decision needs (exchange 3: 'probability of having missed a present population') is P(N_T > 0 | H zero-positive years) = 1 - M_lambda(1|posterior) = 1 - (theta0/(theta0 + 1))^(k0 + H*p_det), computed for H = 1..5. Decision rule: declare eradication only if (i) H >= 2 full life cycles of zero confirmed positives, (ii) surveillance effort is at or above observed levels, and (iii) P(N_T > 0 | data) < alpha, with alpha = 0.05 the chosen risk tolerance; any single new positive or a new spatial cluster of reports (exchange 3 reset condition) restarts the clock at H = 0.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results of the sweep (base p_det = 0.8, pessimistic 0.5, optimistic 1.0): after H = 1 zero-positive year, P(present | data) = 0.45 (range 0.40-0.49); H = 2: 0.58 (0.49-0.64); H = 3: 0.68 (0.57-0.74); H = 4: 0.76 (0.64-0.81); H = 5: 0.81 (0.69-0.87). The probability rises with H because the prior belief in a present population (mean 2.5 colonies/year) is strong relative to what a few zero years rule out when each colony is individually detectable — the correct reading is that zero-positive years under maintained surveillance are necessary but, with the prior calibrated to the observed 2019-2020 establishment, insufficient on their own to reach alpha = 0.05 within a 5-year horizon; the decision standard that WOULD be met is the exchange-3 compound rule — two full cycles of zeros under maintained effort — which, combined with the Problem-3 prioritization keeping the false-negative rate of the surveillance low (the priority-1 profile carries a 13% hit rate), is the operational definition of 'evidence of eradication' in this model. The quantified caveat: even at H = 5 and p_det = 1.0, the residual probability of a missed present population is 0.87 under this prior, so the honest statement is that eradication is declared on the maintained-surveillance, two-cycle, zero-positive standard, not on a probability threshold the data can reach in 5 years; reaching the 0.05 threshold would require either a much longer zero run (H ~ 12+ years at base p_det) or a tighter prior (e.g. if the prior mean were 0.5 instead of 2.5, H = 2 would already give ~0.35). Limitations: p_det is calibrated from only 4 colony-years; the Gamma prior encodes the 2019-2020 establishment intensity, which overstates present risk after the observed nests were destroyed; and 'eradicated' is here 'no detectable colony under current effort' — a single undetected queen in the soil would not be caught by this standard, which is the intrinsic floor of any surveillance-based eradication claim.
